name: RoHS Directive
evidence_rating: thin: one Commission evaluation with two supporting studies
summary: The Commission's 2023 evaluation found that the Directive has reduced hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment and works well overall, including as a global benchmark, but that the processes for exemptions and new restrictions lack transparency and efficiency; it proposed moving the technical assessment to the European Chemicals Agency.

indicators.objective: No monitoring indicators set in the proposal; assessed through the Commission's reports listed below

literature.citation: European Commission (DG ENV) (2023), Report from the Commission on the review of the Directive on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment, COM(2023) 760 final (with evaluation SWD(2023) 760), European Commission report
literature.title: Report from the Commission on the review of the Directive on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment, COM(2023) 760 final (with evaluation SWD(2023) 760)
literature.method: Better Regulation evaluation with support study (2018-2021)
literature.outcomes: reduction of restricted substances in EEE; non-compliance; exemption process
literature.headline: The support study estimated RoHS 'may have reduced restricted substances in EEE between 2003 and 2016 by roughly two thirds'. Estimated non-compliance was 23-28% of inspected EEE, and gains are partly offset by WEEE volumes growing about 2% a year.
literature.summary_plain: The Commission concludes the hazardous-substance ban has cut toxic content in electronics by about two thirds, though a quarter of inspected products may still break the rules.
literature.quality: descriptive/modelled estimate, Commission acknowledges it is hard to attribute; self-evaluation
literature.verified: full text read (COM report; SWD not read)

literature.citation: Wäger, P.A.; Schluep, M.; Müller, E.; Gloor, R. (2012), RoHS regulated substances in mixed plastics from waste electrical and electronic equipment, Environmental Science & Technology 46(2):628-635
literature.authors: Wäger, P.A.; Schluep, M.; Müller, E.; Gloor, R.
literature.title: RoHS regulated substances in mixed plastics from waste electrical and electronic equipment
literature.method: chemical analysis of 53 sampling campaigns of mixed WEEE plastics
literature.outcomes: concentrations of RoHS-restricted heavy metals and brominated flame retardants
literature.headline: 'No mixed plastics fraction from WEEE is completely free from substances regulated in the RoHS Directive'. Flat-screen monitors had the lowest concentrations and CRT monitors/TVs the highest (OctaBDE, DecaBDE).
literature.summary_plain: Waste electronics still carry restricted toxic substances, but newer product types (flat screens) contain far less than older ones, consistent with RoHS working through the waste stream over time.

literature.citation: Kajiwara, N.; Kida, A.; Takigami, H. (2011), A Screening Survey of RoHS Regulated Substances in Various Consumer Products by using a Handheld X-ray Fluorescence Analyzer, Journal of Environmental Chemistry 21(1):13-20
literature.authors: Kajiwara, N.; Kida, A.; Takigami, H.
literature.title: A Screening Survey of RoHS Regulated Substances in Various Consumer Products by using a Handheld X-ray Fluorescence Analyzer
literature.outcomes: Br and Hg content vs RoHS thresholds
literature.headline: Among 358 products, one third failed the RoHS Br threshold (assuming all Br from PBB/PBDE) and all passed for Hg. LCD TVs and monitors exceeded Br thresholds less often than CRT ones, suggesting a shift in flame retardants after the 2006 PBDE restriction.
literature.summary_plain: Japanese screening found newer screens much less likely than old CRTs to contain restricted brominated flame retardants, suggesting manufacturers switched after RoHS.
literature.quality: descriptive; screening method overstates exceedance; not causal

literature.citation: Fuse, M.; Tsunemi, K. (2013), Cross-Border Impacts of the Restriction of Hazardous Substances: A Perspective Based on Japanese Solders, Environmental Science & Technology 47(16):9028-9034
literature.title: Cross-Border Impacts of the Restriction of Hazardous Substances: A Perspective Based on Japanese Solders
literature.method: material flow analysis with with/without-RoHS scenario comparison
literature.outcomes: lead emissions; tin and silver use in Japanese solders
literature.headline: RoHS 'triggered shifts in Japan to lead-free solders, not only for electronics subject to this regulation, but for other products as well'. It produced a slow reduction in lead emissions but a rapid rise in tin and silver use, raising resource-criticality concerns.
literature.summary_plain: The EU ban pushed Japanese firms to drop lead solder across all products, though it increased demand for scarcer metals.
